title: 95% of AI Programs Deliver Little or No Return. Most Fail for a Reason Banks Don’t Expect.
summary: Discover why 95% of AI programs fail, and the sequencing fix most banks overlook.
body_text: Models work. Use cases deliver value. And yet, according to MIT NANDA, as many as 95% of organizations are still seeing little or no return on their AI investments.* The reason is rarely the one banks expect. This is not a problem of ideas or technical capability. In most cases, it comes down to something more basic: the order in which organisations try to scale. That shift, from experimentation to industrialization, is where many banks are now getting stuck. As we explored in AI industrialization vs transformation: How banks move from pilots to scale , the challenge facing banks is no longer whether AI works. It’s whether it can be run, repeatedly and reliably, at scale. Most AI programs fail in the same place A model works in a controlled environment. A use case delivers value. The business responds in a predictable way: scale it, replicate it, build more. Thats where things begin to change. The conditions that made the initial success possible—limited integration, curated data, contained scope—no longer hold. The same model is now expected to operate across multiple systems, processes, and decision points. Complexity increases faster than capability. What looked like acceleration starts to create friction. Delivery slows. Costs become harder to explain. Governance effort expands. At that point, many banks assume they have a scaling problem. In reality, they have a sequencing problem. The question is how to scale without creating drag. Banks scale AI in the wrong order Most banks scaling AI follow a fairly similar evolution consisting of four stages. Yet whether these banks recognize and plan for this evolution or submit to it unwillingly—after some degree of trial and error—is what separates the best in class from the rest. 1. Prove value, but contain the complexity Early AI work should focus on demonstrating value. That typically means working in controlled environments, limiting dependencies, and prioritizing speed over scalability. This is where confidence is built. The risk at this stage is assuming that success in isolation will translate directly into success at scale. 2. Stabilize the foundation before expanding This is the step most organizations delay, and where many programs quietly fail. Not because organizations disagree with the undertaking, but because it’s difficult to justify. Their approach to scaling AI does not produce immediate revenue or visible outcomes. It looks like cost, and it can feel like lost momentum. It’s the equivalent of reinforcing the foundations after the first few floors are already built. From the outside, progress appears to pause. But this step is what allows the building to continue. It can mean the difference between building a skyscraper and being forced to stop at three stories. When this step is skipped, the need doesn’t disappear. It shows up later, when systems are already under pressure and much harder to change. 3. Scale selectively, not broadly Once the underlying environment is stable enough, expansion becomes viable, but it needs to be controlled. At this stage, the goal isn’t more use cases. It’s easier use cases. That only happens if teams stop rebuilding from scratch, leveraging shared environments, consistent processes, and governance that can be reused rather than recreated. Progress here is measured in repeatability, not volume. 4. Industrialize through repetition At this stage, AI becomes part of how the organization operates. New use cases are delivered into an environment that’s already designed to support them. Outcomes become more predictable. The cost and effort of scaling both stabilize. Scale is no longer something that must be forced. It becomes a property of the system. Where your programs are probably going wrong Without deliberate sequencing, a familiar pattern emerges. Pilot success drives expansion. Multiple initiatives are launched in parallel. The underlying environment is expected to catch up. Instead, complexity builds, and delivery slows. As a result, AI efforts shift from building new capabilities to managing what already exists. By the time this pattern becomes visible, it’s already difficult to unwind. The trade-off most banks try to avoid Scaling AI is not just a technical challenge, but a sequencing decision. It requires a different kind of discipline. Leaders need to be deliberate about where they accelerate, and where they invest ahead of visible demand. They need to recognize that some of the most important work may not show immediate returns but will in fact determine whether returns are possible at all. It also requires organizations to measure progress differently—not just in what has been delivered, but in how easily it can be repeated. Avoiding that trade-off doesn’t remove it. It simply delays it to a point where it becomes more expensive to resolve. The order determines the outcome Most banks will move through these stages in some form. The question is whether they do it early, when it’s controlled, or later, when it’s disruptive. AI rarely fails because the models don’t work. It fails when organizations try to scale before the environment is ready to support what they have already built. And by the time that disconnect becomes clear, the cost of correcting it is significantly higher than getting the sequence right in the first place. * Challapally, A., Pease, C., Raskar, R., & Chari, P. (2025, July). The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025 . MIT NANDA.

title: EA SPORTS™ presents Beckham, Zidane and Zlatan in conversation for the first time.
summary: EA SPORTS™ Presents Icons of Football brings together David Beckham, Zinédine Zidane and Zlatan Ibrahimović for a first-ever football conversation, premiering July 18.
body_text: EA SPORTS™ presents Beckham, Zidane and Zlatan together for the first time. Three football icons. One exclusive conversation. Streaming July 18, 2026 on YouTube and Spotify. Cross-border payments require understanding local regulations while meeting the expectations of international workers. ‍ The best international payroll software transforms this challenge from a monthly headache into a streamlined process. Automated systems handle currency conversions, ensure tax compliance, and process payments so companies can focus on building their teams instead of wrestling with spreadsheets and regulations. Whether hiring the first remote worker abroad or scaling a distributed team, the right payroll software makes all the difference. According to the Global Payroll Payments Report 2025, 46% of global workers have experienced payroll payment delays, and 38% reported receiving incorrect payment amounts. These aren't minor inconveniences. They disrupt cash flow, erode trust, and turn straightforward compensation into a financial obstacle course where workers absorb costs through transfer fees, unfavorable exchange rates, and unpredictable processing times. Payroll complexity increased dramatically across global operations in the past year. Strada's 2025 Global Payroll Complexity Index found that 95% of global payroll leaders report increased complexity, driven by multiplying regulations, new reporting requirements, and constantly changing tax treaties. What worked last quarter might not work this quarter, and companies managing workers across 10 countries face 10 different regulatory frameworks, each with its own audit-trail requirements and compliance landmines. Real-time payment access has become the preferred standard among international workers. Niural's 2025 global payroll research found that 60% of employees prefer real-time access to pay over traditional payment schedules. Workers want visibility into when their earnings will arrive, not vague promises about processing times. Predictable payment schedules, transparent status updates, and consistent processing windows build trust faster than competitive rates, and when payments arrive late or require follow-up inquiries, workers start questioning whether the relationship is worth maintaining. AI-powered payroll systems dramatically reduce compliance violations that delay worker payments. The same Neural research found that AI-powered systems achieve a 70% reduction in compliance violations, which directly affects how quickly workers can access their funds without regulatory holds or documentation requests. These capabilities shift control back to workers, letting them decide how and when to convert currencies rather than accepting whatever exchange rate gets applied during processing. Worker classification errors create cascading financial and legal problems for both parties. Misclassification between employee and contractor status affects tax withholding, benefits eligibility, and legal protections. The mistakes can trigger penalties, back taxes, and legal disputes that cost far more than the original payment, yet many workers don't understand how their classification status determines their tax obligations and legal protections until problems arise. Payroll software addresses these challenges by consolidating multi-country payments, compliance tracking, and currency management into unified systems that reduce processing time and eliminate the coordination overhead causing most payment delays. Why International Payroll Management Matters More Than Most Workers Realize Payment turns work into real money for rent , groceries , and survival . For workers from other countries, that money navigates multiple layers : cross-border transfers , currency conversions , and government regulations . Whether payment proceeds smoothly or faces delays depends on how well payroll systems manage this complexity . ‍ Dollar sign icon representing payment transformation ‍ 🎯 Key Point: International workers face multiple payment barriers that domestic employees never encounter, making reliable payroll systems absolutely critical for their financial stability. ‍ " Cross-border payments can involve up to 5-7 intermediary banks , each adding potential delays and fees that impact when workers actually receive their earnings." — International Payment Processing Report, 2024 ‍ Three-layered icons showing payment processing complexity ‍ ⚠️ Warning: Payment delays for international workers don't just mean inconvenience—they can mean the difference between making rent payments on time or facing serious financial hardship in a foreign country. How do payment delays impact your bottom line? Cross-border payments move through correspondent banks , clearing houses, and compliance checkpoints before reaching your account. According to the Global Payroll Payments Report 2025 , 68% of companies report that payment delays affect employee satisfaction. Each intermediary adds fees, processing time, and conversion costs that reduce earnings. A contractor expecting $3,000 might receive $2,750 after transfer fees and unfavorable exchange rates. What hidden costs erode your international payments? The hidden erosion happens quietly. You negotiate a rate and assume the agreed amount will land in your account. Your payment sits in processing limbo for five days while you wait to pay bills. The exchange rate shifts unfavorably between the invoice date and the payment date. Withdrawal fees take another bite when you convert funds to local currency. These friction costs accumulate over months and years, transforming straightforward compensation into a financial obstacle course. Why do workers bear the consequences of poor payroll systems? Most international workers lack the negotiating power of larger companies to secure better payment terms. You accept the payment method your employer or client offers, even when it costs you money or time. If their payroll system sends payments through expensive channels, you bear those costs. If compliance processes delay onboarding, your first payment gets pushed back weeks. The power imbalance means workers rarely question payment infrastructure until problems become severe. How do communication gaps worsen payroll problems? Employers focused on operational efficiency may not realize how payment delays affect worker cash flow . Workers hesitant to seem difficult won't speak up about frustration with fees or timing. Problems persist because neither side understands what the other faces or what matters most to them. What does invisible payroll infrastructure look like? When payroll infrastructure works well, it becomes invisible. Payments arrive predictably, fees are transparent, and currency conversions happen at reasonable rates. Platforms like Ontop handle the complexity behind the scenes: automating compliance checks, optimizing payment routes, and providing visibility into processing timelines so workers know exactly when funds will arrive. How does effective payroll management impact daily life? The difference shows up in daily life. You can commit to rent payments confidently without maintaining large cash buffers for unexpected delays. You spend less time checking payment status and more time focused on work. These are basic expectations that good payroll management should deliver, but often doesn't in international arrangements . What Is International Payroll Management? International payroll management is the comprehensive system that allows companies to legally hire, classify, onboard, pay, and retain workers across multiple countries while following complex regulations . It coordinates tax obligations , employment law , currency conversion , banking networks , and documentation requirements to ensure workers in different locations receive accurate, timely payments without exposing either party to legal or financial risk . ‍ Globe icon representing international payroll management 🎯 Key Point: International payroll management serves as the critical bridge between global workforce expansion and regulatory compliance , ensuring your business can scale internationally without legal complications . ‍ "Companies with effective international payroll systems reduce compliance risks by 85% and improve employee satisfaction scores by 40% compared to those managing payroll manually across borders." — Global Payroll Association, 2024 ‍ Handshake scene representing the bridge between global workforce expansion and regulatory compliance ‍ 💡 Essential Components: The core elements of international payroll management include tax calculation engines , multi-currency processing , local compliance monitoring , and real-time reporting systems that work together to create a seamless global payment infrastructure. The Components That Make Cross-Border Payroll Work Before a payment reaches a worker's account, several processes must align across different legal and financial systems . How does worker classification impact payroll compliance? How a worker is classified determines whether they are an employee or contractor under local law. This affects tax withholding , eligibility for benefits, and legal protections. Misclassification can result in penalties, back taxes, and legal liability. What role does contract documentation play in cross-border payments? Contract documentation establishes payment terms, scope of work, termination conditions, and dispute resolution procedures . Clear agreements aligned with local employment standards help prevent problems when expectations diverge. How do tax compliance requirements vary across jurisdictions? Tax compliance rules vary significantly by location. Some countries require employers to withhold taxes from paychecks, while others make workers responsible for paying their own taxes. Payroll systems must calculate taxes, maintain records, and sometimes remit funds to the government. Rules differ based on worker location, company structure, and pay frequency. What challenges does banking coordination create for international payroll? Banking coordination connects different financial institutions, payment systems, and currency exchanges. A payment might pass through a local bank, correspondent banks, clearing houses, and foreign exchange providers before reaching its destination. Each intermediary adds time, fees, and potential failure points. What factors are driving increased global payroll complexity? According to Strada's 2025 Global Payroll Complexity Index , 95% of payroll leaders worldwide report increased complexity in their work over the past year. Rules multiply, countries introduce new reporting requirements, tax treaties shift, and payment networks update their systems regularly. How do currency fluctuations impact international payroll? Changes in currency exchange rates add unpredictability. A worker quoted at $3,000 might receive $2,850 or $3,100, depending on exchange rates and the timing of conversion. Old payroll processes batch transactions, exposing workers to days of rate changes between payment approval and deposit. What compliance risks do different labor laws create? Different labor laws create compliance risks. One country requires 13th-month payments, another has specific severance calculations, and a third enforces strict payment timing with penalties for delays. Companies managing workers across ten countries face ten distinct regulatory frameworks, each with different audit requirements. What are the immediate impacts when payroll systems break down? When payroll infrastructure breaks down, payments arrive late or incomplete, workers lose trust and disengage, and administrative teams spend hours reconciling errors instead of doing strategic work. Our payroll software prevents these issues by ensuring reliable, on-time payments and reducing manual reconciliation work. ‍ The financial cost is measurable; the reputational cost is often more damaging. Contractors experiencing repeated payment issues decline future projects, warn peers, or disappear without explanation. Companies lose access to talent they've already invested in training. What legal risks do payroll failures create? Compliance failures carry legal risk. Tax authorities don't accept "we didn't know" as a defense. Misclassification lawsuits can last for years and cost millions of pounds, creating exposure that sophisticated companies work hard to avoid. ‍ Most workers don't encounter these systems until something goes wrong. The exact details vary by country and provider , but the patterns repeat with uncomfortable consistency. ‍ Globe surrounded by payroll problem icons showing global consistency ‍ 🎯 Key Point: Despite geographical differences, global workers consistently report the same core payroll issues regardless of their location or payment platform. ‍ "The patterns of payroll problems repeat across borders in a way that is uncomfortable and consistent for remote workers worldwide." ‍ Three cards showing common payroll problems: late payments, hidden fees, and complex processes ‍ ⚠️ Warning: These recurring payroll issues aren't isolated incidents—they represent systemic problems that affect millions of global workers daily, creating unnecessary stress and financial uncertainty. What causes payment delays in international payroll? Payment delays create mounting financial stress with each passing day. ‍ According to The Global Payroll Payments Report 2025 , 46% of global workers have experienced payroll payment delays. International banking systems process transactions at different speeds, manual approval workflows create bottlenecks, and currency conversions require additional verification steps. How do payment delays impact workers and contractors? Workers who need to pay rent, buy groceries, or make loan payments cannot afford to wait while their money moves through systems they don't control. ‍ Freelancers and contractors face extra delays across multiple income sources. A three-day delay from one client and a five-day delay from another create a ten-day gap that disrupts every financial commitment. Predicting when money will arrive matters as much as the payment amount itself. What hidden costs reduce worker payments? The contract states one number. The bank account shows another, smaller one. ‍ Wire transfer fees, intermediary bank charges, currency conversion spreads , and account maintenance costs reduce the amount workers receive. A $3,000 invoice might arrive as $2,750. These deductions often aren't disclosed up front, and workers discover them only after reviewing their statements. ‍ Over time, accumulated losses become significant, particularly for those receiving weekly or biweekly payments, where fees are applied repeatedly. How do exchange rate markups create additional costs? Some payment providers hide costs in exchange rates instead of showing explicit fees. The difference between the interbank rate and the applied rate can represent a hidden markup of 2% to 4% , ranging from $60 to $120 on a $3,000 payment. Incorrect Payment Amounts and Reconciliation Headaches Numbers should be straightforward. Often they aren't. ‍ Research from The Global Payroll Payments Report 2025 found that 38% of workers reported receiving incorrect payment amounts. Calculation errors, misapplied tax withholdings, currency conversion mistakes, and contract misinterpretations cause these discrepancies. Resolving them requires documentation, email exchanges, and follow-up requests that can take weeks, leaving workers short on funds they've already earned. ‍ Recurring errors signal a systemic problem and erode trust in the payment relationship. Workers question whether they'll be paid correctly next time, affecting how they plan their finances and whether to continue working together. Administrative Friction That Delays Everything Getting paid shouldn't require extensive paperwork. Yet many international payment systems require repeated documentation, unclear contract terms, missing tax forms, and onboarding procedures that drag on for weeks. Workers submit the same information multiple times because different departments fail to communicate. ‍ Platforms like payroll software centralize documentation and automate compliance checks, reducing onboarding from weeks to days. Our payroll solution treats administrative requirements as a technical problem to solve rather than a burden to pass on to workers. Lack of Visibility Into Payment Status Once a payment is processed, it enters a black box. Workers cannot see where it is, which institution is handling it, or when it will arrive. This uncertainty makes financial planning nearly impossible. ‍ This lack of openness creates stress beyond the immediate payment. Workers cannot confidently commit to expenses, schedule bill payments, or make financial decisions without knowing when earnings will arrive. The lack of transparency turns every payment cycle into a guessing game, affecting how workers evaluate opportunities and manage their relationships with employers or clients. title: An overview of Context Propagation in OpenTelemetry
summary: OpenTelemetry context propagation: how propagators, W3C Trace Context, and baggage carry trace context across services. Setup and examples for SigNoz.
body_text: An overview of Context Propagation in OpenTelemetry Published on: May 15, 2024 Last Updated: July 06, 2026 8 min read To effectively manage modern applications, you need to understand how they work on the inside. Distributed tracing is the key to this, providing a detailed picture of a request's journey across every service. OpenTelemetry has emerged as the industry-standard framework for implementing tracing and achieving true observability in complex, distributed systems. In this article, we embark on a journey to explore the core concept of context propagation within Open Telemetry . We'll dissect its significance, delve into its mechanics, and uncover the mechanisms it employs. The Fundamentals of Context Propagation Context propagation is fundamental to OpenTelemetry's tracing. It's the mechanism for transmitting essential trace and span contexts across services in a distributed application, ensuring every operation is linked to its origin. Trace Context Trace context represents the overarching journey of a request or transaction across various services and components in a distributed system. It includes: Trace ID : A unique identifier for the entire trace. Timestamps : Precise timing information for trace and span creation. Baggage Items : Optional key-value pairs for additional context. Span Context Span context focuses on individual spans within a trace, representing specific operations or units of work. It includes: Span ID : A unique identifier for each span within the trace. Trace ID : The same trace ID as in the trace context, linking spans to the broader trace. Timestamps : Timing details for span creation. These contexts work together to provide a complete framework for tracing and correlating requests as they move through distributed systems. Now, let's delve into the inner workings of context propagation in OpenTelemetry. The Journey of a Trace from Instrumentation to Export Explained Scope of this guide: this page focuses on how OpenTelemetry implements context propagation, the propagator API, the W3C Trace Context (traceparent and tracestate) headers, and baggage, with setup for your SDK. To understand the underlying concept (what context propagation is and why distributed traces depend on it), check out our dedicated context propagation in distributed tracing guide , which covers that foundation. The process of context propagation in OpenTelemetry can be broken down into several key steps: 1. Instrumentation The first step is instrumentation , which involves integrating the OpenTelemetry SDK into your application. This can be done with auto-instrumentation libraries for many popular frameworks and languages, often requiring little to no code changes or manual instrumentation depending on the amount of telemetry data you want to collect. Instrumentation is the gateway for OpenTelemetry to collect telemetry data, as it captures specific events and operations as spans within a trace. 2. Context Creation Once your application is instrumented, OpenTelemetry automatically handles context creation. This involves generating a unique trace context and span context (explained in the previous section) for each request. These contexts include unique identifiers (trace and span IDs) and timestamps, which are essential for uniquely identifying every trace and span and carrying the necessary metadata. 3. Propagation Mechanisms With the context created, it needs to be transmitted between services. This is where propagation mechanisms come in. OpenTelemetry supports various methods for this, discussed in the next section. For text-based protocols like HTTP, this process is managed by a Trace Context Text Map Propagator . This component is responsible for injecting the trace context into the headers of an outgoing request and extracting it on the receiving end. Text map is a simple key-value store where both keys and values are strings. In the context of web services, HTTP headers are a common example of a text map. The choice of propagation mechanism depends on your application's architecture. These mechanisms are the conduits through which the trace and span context travel as a request flows through your system. 4. Custom Span Creation and Data Collection As the context is propagated, developers can create custom spans to represent individual units of work within the application. These spans are linked together by the propagated context, forming a complete trace. Within each span, OpenTelemetry collects a wealth of telemetry data, including timing information, events, and other details that are crucial for understanding system behavior and performance. 5. Exporting Telemetry Data The final step is exporting telemetry data. OpenTelemetry sends the collected data to a backend system, such as a tracing database or an observability platform like SigNoz. This is where the data is analyzed and visualized, allowing you to troubleshoot issues, optimize performance, and gain a deeper understanding of your application. The Varied Landscape of Context Propagation Mechanisms 1. HTTP Headers HTTP headers are commonly employed for context propagation in web-based applications. They offer a straightforward way to carry trace and span context between HTTP requests and responses. Two essential HTTP headers are used for this purpose: traceparent : This header contains the trace and span IDs, ensuring that context is consistently transferred along with each HTTP request. tracestate : The tracestate header is used for additional contextual information, such as baggage items. It allows developers to include custom key-value pairs to enrich the context of a trace. 2. gRPC Metadata In systems utilizing gRPC for communication, gRPC metadata is the chosen mechanism for context propagation. Similar to HTTP headers, gRPC metadata includes trace and span context information. OpenTelemetry seamlessly integrates with gRPC, enabling the straightforward propagation of context within gRPC-based microservices. 3. Message Queues In message-driven architectures, where systems communicate through message queues like Apache Kafka or RabbitMQ, context propagation is achieved by embedding trace context within messages . Each message carries trace and span IDs, allowing for the correlation of events and the tracing of messages as they traverse the messaging system. 4. Custom Propagation In certain scenarios, you might find it necessary to implement custom context propagation mechanisms tailored to your specific requirements. OpenTelemetry's flexibility allows you to design custom approaches for transmitting context information that aligns with your application's unique needs. These mechanisms are vital for maintaining visibility and traceability in distributed systems, enhancing observability and troubleshooting capabilities across services and components. Manual Context Propagation: Taking Control In some scenarios, you might find it necessary to take manual control of context propagation, especially when dealing with unique requirements or communication patterns. Let's explore a simplified example to illustrate how manual context propagation can be implemented: Imagine two microservices, Service A and Service B, communicating via RabbitMQ. Service A needs to propagate context information along with a message to Service B: # Service A: Sending a message with trace context from opentelemetry import trace from opentelemetry . trace . propagation . tracecontext import TraceContextTextMapPropagator carrier = { } # Create a span for the current operation in Service A with trace . get_tracer ( __name__ ) . start_as_current_span ( "Operation in Service A" ) as span : # Write the current context into the carrier. # A TextMapPropagator works with any dict-like object as its Carrier by default. TraceContextTextMapPropagator ( ) . inject ( carrier ) # Attach trace context to the message message = { "content" : "Hello, Service B!" , "trace_context" : carrier } # Publish the message to RabbitMQ rabbitmq_publisher . publish ( message ) In Service B, upon receiving the message, we extract the trace context and continue the trace: # Service B: Receiving and extracting trace context from the message from opentelemetry import trace def process_message ( message ) : # Extract the trace context from the received message carrier = message . get ( "trace_context" ) ctx = TraceContextTextMapPropagator ( ) . extract ( carrier = carrier ) # Create a new span in Service B using the extracted trace context with trace . get_tracer ( __name__ ) . start_as_current_span ( "Operation in Service B" , context = ctx ) : # Your code for processing the message here This concise example demonstrates how manual context propagation allows for precise control over tracing in distributed systems. It shows how trace context can be extracted from one service and applied to another, enabling seamless tracing continuity. Conclusion In conclusion, context propagation in OpenTelemetry forms the basis of passing essential information with a request across network boundaries and processes. By understanding the inner workings and various propagation mechanisms, organizations can harness the power of OpenTelemetry to gain actionable insights, troubleshoot effectively, and optimize their applications for peak performance. Once you have collected data with OpenTelemetry, you can use a backend like SigNoz to store and analyze your OpenTelemetry data. SigNoz is an OpenTelemetry-native APM built to provide the best visualizations for OpenTelemetry data. Traces and spans as visualised in SigNoz Getting started with SigNoz SigNoz Cloud is the easiest way to run SigNoz. Sign up for a free account and get 30 days of unlimited access to all features. You can also install and self-host SigNoz yourself since it is open-source. With 24,000+ GitHub stars, open-source SigNoz is loved by developers. Find the instructions to self-host SigNoz. To further build an understanding of concepts, see our guide to OpenTelemetry tracing for how traces are produced end to end, and learn how spans in distributed tracing capture individual units of work. For the bigger picture, our overview of distributed tracing explains the core ideas, while our roundup of distributed tracing tools helps you compare options. If you run services at scale, microservices observability shows how tracing ties requests together across boundaries, and OpenTelemetry vs Jaeger weighs two common approaches to collecting and storing that data. title: Scaling organisations making AI go well
summary: Billions in new funding is fueling rapid growth at AI safety organisations, but they're struggling to hire COOs, chiefs of staff, and programme managers. If you have AI safety context and operations skills, this could be your most impactful path.
body_text: Some AI safety knowledge is critical We often hear from readers asking how much AI safety knowledge they need for these roles, and why it’s so essential for getting hired. Experienced professionals are (understandably) sometimes confused or frustrated when they apply for an AI safety job that fits their background, but are rejected early in the process. They may have written a few short answer responses in the application or had an interview that tested their knowledge of and interest in AI safety, only to get a vague rejection. Often, they insufficiently communicated an understanding of the organisation’s priorities, or knowledge about AI safety in general. This is sometimes referred to as having a lack of ‘ context .’ We think there are (at least) three reasons why hiring managers often prioritise preexisting AI safety knowledge and motivation in their senior operations and strategy hires: Understanding why decisions are made, not just how : growing an organisation involves many judgement calls about org-wide priorities, and sometimes requires standing in for existing leadership. The AI safety field’s strategic aims don’t map cleanly onto normal nonprofit or startup logic. Teams who believe humanity could go extinct in the next ten years due to an intelligence explosion , or that the main beneficiaries of their work could be future digital minds , will probably allocate resources and make decisions in different ways than others. Even organisations that work on more immediate AI security or misuse issues often have small teams, so want their senior staff to have a good internal model of the field as a whole to be able to take on strategic responsibilities. Culture fit and enjoyment of the work: mission-oriented organisations often build high-trust environments around shared values. For example, if you want to join a climate nonprofit or political party, you should decide whether you’d enjoy the culture you’d be joining. You’ll do better work and be happier if you believe in an organisation’s mission, and they want to hire people who do. This takes time to train : the field is still relatively small, with a lot of tacit knowledge that takes time to absorb. Many staff feel crunched by urgent problems in their daily work, so are hesitant to invest extra time into training. Still, some organisations are building this into their onboarding process by running reading and discussion groups, sending staff to conferences, and using more internal staff mentorship. In practice, applying this knowledge could look like: deciding which organisations or media outlets to partner with to achieve a shared goal; designing and executing a fundraising strategy for potential donors interested in AI safety; leading high-touch hiring rounds for top talent; or determining what the organisation’s risk tolerance should be for concerns like public relations, opportunity costs of moving too slowly, budgeting given your organisation’s estimates around AI progress, etc. Of course, the kind of knowledge and motivation required will differ across organisations. Some organisations have detailed worldviews and theories of change that affect all of their work ( MIRI , for example), while others work across many research areas and have less of a defined ‘house view’ ( CSET , for example). The organisations on our job board have different approaches to making AI go well, so we’d encourage you to read their websites carefully before applying. In addition, the more well-scoped a position with an organisation is, such as building HR or IT systems, the lower the bar will typically be for this.

title: Messaging App Go To Market Strategy: A Practical Framework
summary: This guide lays out a practical messaging app go to market strategy, covering positioning, launch sequencing, monetization timing, and the infrastructure
body_text: Launching a messaging app is one of the hardest go-to-market problems in software. Chat apps only work when the people someone actually talks to are also on the app, which means a messaging product with 10,000 downloads and no adoption within any single friend group or team is functionally worthless to its users. This is why messaging apps live or die on go-to-market strategy far more than on feature depth. Most founders overinvest in features like disappearing messages, reactions, or AI summaries, and underinvest in the sequencing question: who needs to be on this app first, and why would the next person join after them. This guide lays out a practical messaging app go to market strategy , covering positioning, launch sequencing, monetization timing, and the infrastructure decisions that determine whether the go-to-market plan is even executable. TL;DR Messaging apps need a network-first go-to-market strategy , not a feature-first one. Adoption depends on getting whole conversation groups to move together. Pick a specific wedge use case rather than trying to be a general WhatsApp alternative from day one. Sequence the launch around a closed community first , then expand outward once retention within that group is proven. Monetization should wait until engagement is proven , since messaging apps depend on trust and premature monetization kills adoption. Technical reliability is part of go-to-market , not separate from it. Message delivery failures and call drops during a launch window are what kill word of mouth. Launching on proven, pre-built messaging infrastructure removes the biggest execution risk, letting the team focus entirely on the go-to-market motion instead of core chat reliability. Why Messaging App Go To Market Strategy Needs A Different Playbook Most SaaS products can succeed with a single user adopting them. A messaging app cannot. Its entire value proposition is relational, which means the go-to-market motion has to solve a coordination problem before it solves a feature problem. This changes what matters at launch. A project management tool can win a single user with individual productivity features. A messaging app has to convince an entire group, family, team, or community, to move together, or it fails no matter how good the individual features are. This is why go-to-market planning for messaging apps needs to start with the network, not the product. Start With a Wedge, Not a Whole Market Trying to launch as a general-purpose WhatsApp or Telegram competitor from day one is a losing strategy for almost every new entrant. Those platforms already have the network effect locked in, and a generic alternative gives users no reason to switch. A wedge-first approach works better, and it means starting with a narrow use case where an existing messaging app is a bad fit. Vertical-specific communities , like real estate agents coordinating with clients, gig workers coordinating with dispatchers, or gaming communities that need low-latency voice alongside chat. Regional or regulatory gaps , where compliance, data residency, or local payment integration make an existing global app inconvenient. Embedded messaging inside an existing product , where chat is a feature of a marketplace, delivery platform, or social app rather than a standalone destination. Underserved demographics , such as enterprise teams that need message retention and compliance controls that consumer apps do not offer. The wedge does not need to be permanent. WhatsApp itself started as a simple status-sharing app before pivoting into messaging. The point of a wedge is to get a real, retained network established before expanding into a broader messaging use case. Sequence the Launch Around Closed Communities Once the wedge is chosen, the launch sequence matters more than the marketing budget. Messaging apps that succeed almost always launch inside a closed, high-trust community first, prove retention there, and then expand outward. A workable sequencing approach looks like this. Start with one tightly connected group where most members already talk to each other daily, such as a single company, a college cohort, or a niche professional community. Get the group to fully migrate , not partially. Partial migration means the group keeps using the old app for some conversations, which kills the new app’s utility. Watch retention and message volume within that group before expanding to a second group. If the first group does not stick, expanding the user base will not fix the underlying product-network fit problem. Expand through referral paths that mirror real relationships , like invite flows that pull in a user’s actual contacts rather than generic sharing links. This is slower than a broad paid acquisition push, but it is the only sequencing that actually works for relational products. Broad acquisition without network density just produces a large number of users who each have nobody to talk to on the app. Delay Monetization Until Trust and Retention Are Proven Monetizing a messaging app too early is one of the most common go-to-market mistakes. Messaging is a trust-dependent category. Users need to believe the app is reliable and not going to disappear or start charging unpredictably before they will commit their primary conversations to it. Avoid paywalling core chat and call functionality during the early growth phase, since this directly undermines the migration decision users are being asked to make. Introduce monetization through adjacent value , like business messaging tools, premium broadcast channels, or in-chat commerce features, once a base of engaged users exists. Consider monetization paths that align with usage patterns already seen in the market , such as WhatsApp’s own move into business APIs and in-chat payments, rather than generic subscription paywalls. Treat early monetization experiments as signal-gathering , not primary revenue, until daily active usage and retention numbers justify a real pricing push. The apps that get this sequencing wrong tend to see a spike in downloads followed by a steep drop-off, because the perceived risk of committing conversations to a paywalled or unstable product outweighs the convenience it offers. Technical Reliability Is a Go-To-Market Requirement, Not a Later Concern A go-to-market plan for a messaging app can be executed flawlessly on the marketing side and still fail if the underlying product cannot deliver messages reliably, drops calls, or lags under concurrent load during a launch window. For messaging apps specifically, technical reliability functions as part of the go-to-market strategy, not a separate engineering workstream. Word of mouth is the primary growth channel for any messaging app. A single bad group chat experience during a launch spreads faster than any marketing campaign can compensate for. This is where a lot of otherwise well-planned messaging app launches fall apart. Building real-time chat infrastructure , message delivery guarantees, audio and video calling, and group messaging at reliable scale is a deep engineering problem, and most founders underestimate how long it takes to get right from scratch. Comparison: Custom-Built Messaging App vs. Pre-Built Infrastructure Factor Custom Build From Scratch Appscrip’s Pre-Built WhatsApp Clone Time to market 6-12 months 45-60 days Cost to launch $100,000-$200,000+ Starts at $8,000 Message delivery and encryption Built and hardened over time End-to-end encryption and PCI-DSS compliance included Audio and video calling Requires separate WebRTC integration effort Built in with group audio and video calling Source code ownership Full ownership, full build burden 100% ownership after full payment Go-to-market focus Split between infrastructure and growth Fully on positioning, sequencing, and community launch Why Infrastructure Choice Determines Go-To-Market Speed The single biggest lever a messaging app founder has over their own go-to-market timeline is how much time gets spent building core chat infrastructure versus executing the actual launch strategy. Real-time messaging, encrypted calls, and group chat reliability take most engineering teams six months or more to get production-ready, and that is time not spent on the community-first launch sequencing that actually determines adoption. Appscrip’s messaging app platform is built specifically to remove this bottleneck: Core messaging and calling infrastructure already built , including one-on-one and group chat, audio and video calls, and media sharing, so the team is not starting from zero on the hardest technical problem. End-to-end encryption and PCI-DSS compliance included , which matters both for user trust and for any monetization path involving in-chat payments. In-chat money transfer capability built in , useful for wedge use cases in commerce-adjacent or gig-economy communities. Launch in 45-60 days instead of 6-12 months , meaning the go-to-market clock starts months earlier than a custom build would allow. 100% source code ownership , so the go-to-market and product roadmap are never dependent on someone else’s platform decisions. Getting to market faster on proven infrastructure means more of the limited early runway goes toward the wedge, the closed-community launch, and the sequencing work that actually determines whether a messaging app achieves the network density it needs to survive. title: Website visitor tracking: the complete B2B guide
summary: Website visitor tracking has three levels: analytics, company-level, and contact-level. Learn which one your B2B team needs and how to do it compliantly.
body_text: "Website visitor tracking" gets used for a tool that counts pageviews, sessions, and bounce rates. That's analytics. Analytics tells you how many people showed up, which pages they hit, and where they dropped off. It doesn't tell you who they were. For a B2B team, what analytics hides is the stuff that actually moves pipeline. Which company is on your pricing page right now, which person on the buying committee, and how fast you can reach them while they still care. So "how do I track visitors to my website" is really three different questions stacked on top of each other. Answer the wrong one and you buy a dashboard nobody acts on. The levels differ, the identifying part has real privacy rules, and tracking has honest limits you should know before a pilot. What website visitor tracking actually means The phrase covers everything from a free analytics pixel to a full contact-level identity graph, and the gap between those is enormous. Vendors blur it on purpose. A page that promises to "track your website visitors" might mean it counts anonymous sessions, or it might mean it can hand a named person to your sales team. Those are not the same product, and they don't cost the same either. The useful way to think about it is a ladder. Each rung tells you more about the person behind the visit, and each rung is harder to climb. Before you shop for a tool, decide which rung you actually need. Plenty of teams overpay for analytics and underinvest in identity. The three levels of website visitor tracking B2B teams should know which level a tool operates at before they buy: Level one — analytics. Anonymous counts of sessions, sources, and page paths. Level two — company-level identification. Matches a visitor's IP address to a company name. Level three — contact-level de-anonymization. Resolves the individual person by name and title so a rep has someone real to reach out to. Frustration with visitor tracking often comes from buying one level and expecting another. Analytics is good at measuring the site. Company-level is good at telling you a storm is out there somewhere. Only contact-level gives you someone a rep can actually call. Level 1: Analytics and session tracking This is Google Analytics, Plausible, most heatmap tools. It's essential for understanding traffic patterns, conversion rates, and which content pulls its weight. It's also anonymous by design, and increasingly limited by cookie consent and ad blockers. You'll see that 23 people viewed the pricing page, never who they were. Keep analytics for measuring the site, but don't expect it to feed sales a single name. Level 2: Company-level identification Reverse-IP tools and most legacy account-based platforms sit here. They map a visit to a company. "Someone from HP was researching this." The problem is what happens next. A signal that an account visited is not something a rep can act on. If you're calling a thousand-person company and pulling five contacts, the odds you reach the person who was actually on the site are close to zero, and the person who does pick up has no idea what you're talking about. Remote work makes it worse because IP-to-company matching breaks when nobody is in the office. Company-level tracking creates work for sales and rarely ends it, which is why so many teams stop acting on it. Level 3: Contact-level de-anonymization This is the rung that changes the sales conversation. You resolve the anonymous visitor to a named contact, filtered to your ICP, with the pages and ads they touched. Instead of "an account visited," you get "the director of demand gen at a target account viewed pricing twice this week." That is the difference between something a rep acts on and a Slack channel they mute by week two. If you want the mechanics, our guide to how to identify website visitors walks through the reveal step, and contact-level targeting covers why the person, not the logo, is the unit that matters. Contact-level is the only rung that hands sales a person to call, which is the whole point of tracking visitors in the first place. How to track website visitors without tripping privacy rules Identity resolution lives in a real regulatory frame. Skip that, and you get a legal review that kills the project. Two laws set the boundaries for most B2B teams. The EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) governs anyone processing data on EU residents and treats consent as the default requirement. In the US, the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) gives consumers the right to know what's collected and to opt out. Neither law bans visitor identification, but both shape how you can do it. The compliant path has a few moving parts. Identity tools typically use device fingerprinting rather than third-party cookies, which sidesteps the consent-banner problem but doesn't erase your obligations. A US-only scope removes the largest slice of GDPR risk up front. And your own consent-management platform still gates what fires. Run an opt-in banner and your reveal rate will land in the single digits, by design, because that's a tradeoff you're choosing, not a tool failing. Treat privacy as the first design decision, scope to where your ICP actually is, and lead your IT review with security documentation instead of a sales pitch. Turning a revealed visitor into timely outreach Identifying a visitor is worthless if nobody acts on it. The most common failure we see is a tool that dumps every site visitor into a Slack channel with no playbook attached. Within a month, reps have stopped looking. Extra data nobody actions is just clutter. Three things turn a reveal into a conversation. Filter to ICP first. Raw visitor traffic is mostly noise. A recruiter scoping your careers page and a student writing a market report don't belong in a rep's queue. Filter by title, department, and account before anything reaches a person. Attach a next step. A signal without a recommended action gets forgotten. Reps shouldn't have to ask "cool, what do I do with this?" Pair every reveal with a play. Enroll in a specific sequence, retarget with an ad, or route to the account manager. Move while it's warm. Intent decays. A visitor who was on your pricing page today is a different prospect in two weeks. Speed-to-lead is the advantage, so automate the routing instead of relying on someone to cherry-pick a channel. Our breakdown of how to act on buyer interest and the field guide on what to do with intent data both go deeper on building the play. The reveal is the easy part. The filtering and the playbook are what make sales trust it. What website visitor tracking can't tell you Being honest about the limits is how you set expectations before a pilot, not after. Contact-level tracking resolves a percentage of your US traffic, not all of it. A low count often means low ICP-qualified US traffic rather than a broken tool, but it does mean tracking supplements your pipeline rather than replaces it. It won't do reliable lead attribution for a privacy-conscious audience whose pixels fall off fast. It won't reveal visitors outside the US at the contact level today. And it can't tell you why someone visited, only that they did, which is why messaging discipline matters. Reach out about the behavior, the ad they clicked, or the category they're evaluating, rather than "I saw you were on our website." None of that makes tracking less valuable. It makes it a tool with a job. You can see how Vector approaches the identity and activation layer on our product page . Buy visitor tracking for what it does well, resolving and routing real buyers, and don't expect it to carry attribution or coverage it was never built for. Where this leaves you Website visitor tracking covers several products under one label, and the version that grows pipeline is the version that hands sales a name. Analytics measures the site. Company-level identification points at a crowd and hopes someone acts on it. Contact-level de-anonymization gives you the person, and only the person is something a rep can act on. Decide which rung you need, do the identifying part inside the privacy rules instead of around them, and wire every reveal to a filter and a play so the data reaches sales while the visit is still warm.
